title: Black versus Negro as terms
summary: They discuss how "Black" was once derogatory, plus the Indian and Negro as words.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You and I are old enough to remember when to refer to people as "Blacks" was definitely derogatory. I mean, in the Thirties, you... I mean, if I were talking to you in the Thirties I would never refer to Colored people as Blacks, because that was a colonial term. But then we go through a phase where there are Negroes in this country, and then they all want to be called Blacks. I don't really...
Well, the colonial term, especially the American colonial term, had a different, more derogatory name than "Blacks."
Well, it still was pretty (?) in the European countries.

Whether you like it or not, this had the hidden... We will never know what the real history of the American Indian is, and they are reluctant to keep bringing up about the American Indian. That was definitely a way of life here!

We used to joke about people, you know, when they did... Blacks would pay attention to the word. "Black" would be to imitate in a humorous sort of way. Although I was taught to say, "Well, it's better to be in the black

than to be in the red" -- you know? I was saying to you earlier... Actually, what I heard when I came up, you'd always say "the Indians fought and died; the Negroes brimmed(?) and multiplied." So I mean, we were a force to be reckoned with, you know.
After all, "Negro" was merely the Spanish word for "Black."
